1.pericope_label: And after these things I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, that the wind should not blow on the earth, nor on the sea, nor on any tree. And I saw another angel ascending from the east, having the seal of the living God: and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels, to whom it was given to hurt the earth and the sea

schools.summary: State what the chapter is for. Where there had been awful consternation and alarm, as if the end of the world were coming, the signs of the approaching consummation are as it were held back until there should be an opportunity of sealing the number that was to be saved. This is symbolized by four angels standing in the four quarters of the earth, holding the winds and the storms that they should not blow, until the servants of God should be sealed in their foreheads. The idea is of sudden destruction about to burst on the world, which if unrestrained would apparently bring on the consummation of all things, but which is held back until the purposes of God in regard to his people shall be accomplished, that is, until those who are his true servants shall be designated by some appropriate mark; and this furnishes an opportunity of disclosing a glorious vision of those who will be saved, alike among the Jews and the Gentiles. The end of the world does not come at the opening of the sixth seal, as it seemed as if it would: the number of the chosen was not complete, and the impending wrath was therefore suspended. On the second angel, note that he is evidently unconnected with the four and employed for another purpose, and that he too must be symbolic — all that is implied is that something would be done as if an angel had done it. He appeared in the east and seemed to rise like the sun. It is not easy to determine what is the special significancy, if any, of the east here, or why this quarter is designated rather than the north, the south or the west: it may be that as light begins in the east this would be a fit symbol of something to be compared with the light of the morning, or perhaps no special significance is to be attached to the quarter at all, for it is not necessary to suppose that every minute thing in a symbol is to receive a complete fulfilment, or that there will be some particular thing to correspond with it. Perhaps all that is meant is that, as the sun comes forth with splendour from the east, so the angel came with magnificence to perform a task cheerful and joyous like that which the sun performs; and it is certain that from no other quarter would it be so appropriate to represent an angel as coming forth to perform a purpose of light and mercy and salvation. Elsewhere link the chapter to the seal before it. In the sixth seal the winds had blown and had shaken violently the fig-tree, causing its untimely figs to drop off, and those winter figs represented those whose religious life was unequal to the strain of trial, and who failed in the crisis to which they were exposed. But is all the fruit shaken off? No: Christ had said that if a man abide not in him he is cast forth as a branch, but that those who abode in him, purged by their trials, would bring forth more fruit, and fruit that should remain. They would not be as winter figs, easily torn from the boughs, for their strength was in God: before the stormy winds of manifold trials had blown, they had been sealed with the seal of the living God. This is the scene brought before us in this chapter, in which the care of God, who restrains the winds from violence that they should not shake too soon the immature fruit, the tokens by which the sealed are known, and the meaning of their sealing are all set forth. The chapter, in fact, answers the solemn question of the last chapter: who is able to stand? The winds are clearly emblems of days of trouble or judgment. On the second angel, translate, going up from the rising of the sun, having a seal of the living God: this angel rises into view from the door of the dawn, for in the midst of the dark symptoms of coming storm and judgment there springs up a light for the righteous and joyful gladness for such as are true-hearted — they need not be afraid of evil tidings whose hearts stand fast believing in the Lord. The seal is the emblem of security: it was placed on our Lord’s sepulchre to keep the tomb safe from invasion, and the king’s seal was placed on the stone laid at the mouth of the den in which Daniel was imprisoned. The entrusting of the seal into the hands of others was the token that royal authority had been for the time delegated to man, as when Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his seal. Elsewhere again keep to the words. Instead of the seventh seal being opened, two episodes occupy this chapter, the sealing of the servants of God and the vision of the redeemed before the throne. Standing is a second perfect participle, intransitive; corners is the old word for angle; holding is the present participle of the verb to hold fast, and the four winds are held prisoner by angels at each of the four corners — some Jews held the winds from due north, south, east and west to be favourable, while those from the angles were unfavourable. That no wind should blow is a negative purpose clause, lest a wind keep on blowing; and note the accusative with the preposition in the last clause, against any tree, a picture of attack on the tree like a tornado’s path. On the second angel: ascending is a present participle, picturing the process; from the sun-rising means from the east, though why is not told, and it has been suggested that it is because Palestine is east of Patmos. The seal of the living God is here the signet ring, like that used by an Oriental monarch to give validity to official documents, and the use of living accents the eternal life of God as opposed to the ephemeral pagan gods. The angels are here identified with the winds, as the angels of the churches with the churches; and the injury is to come by letting loose the winds, not by withholding them.

Place the vision in time, and then name the angel. After the opening of six of the seals, and after the demolition of heathen deities, heathen worship and heathen magistrates in the Roman empire, John had this vision; it therefore does not refer to the preservation of the Christians before and at the destruction of Jerusalem, which was under the first seal, nor to the security of the saints from the wrath of the Lamb when it fell upon the Pagan worshippers, which was under the sixth seal and was now over, but rather to an intermediate space of time between the sixth and seventh seal, reaching from Constantine to Theodosius. Upon Constantine’s becoming sole emperor the church enjoyed great peace and tranquillity after the blustering storms of Pagan persecution ceased, and great numbers of God’s elect were converted and sealed, and the winds of heathen persecution were held and blew no more, unless for a short time under the Emperor Julian — though the church was not free from the wind of error and heresy, nor from the storms of contention which arose. Then refuse the obvious identification of the second angel. He is not Constantine, who came from the eastern parts to the empire with the true knowledge of God and the authority of God to propagate it, and who repressed the four angels, or evil spirits — contention, ambition, heresy and war — from doing the mischief they otherwise would, and sealed the saints by giving them a platform of doctrine at the council of Nice, as some have thought. It is the uncreated angel, the angel of the covenant, the Lord Jesus Christ. For who but he should have the privy seal of heaven, who is the angel of the great council? And who could speak in such an authoritative manner to the four angels, saying, hurt not the earth, but he who is the head of all principality and power? And who should seal the servants of the Lord, but he who has them in his hands and keeps them by his power, so that none of them shall perish?

Take the winds for errors, and draw the comfort. By these winds we suppose are meant those errors and corruptions in religion which would occasion a great deal of trouble and mischief to the church of God. Sometimes the Holy Spirit is compared to the wind; here the spirits of error are compared to the four winds, contrary one to another, but doing much hurt to the church, the garden and vineyard of God, breaking the branches and blasting the fruits of his plantation. The devil is called the prince of the power of the air; he, by a great wind, overthrew the house of Job’s eldest son; and errors are as wind, by which those who are unstable are shaken and carried to and fro. Observe three things. They are called the winds of the earth, because they blow only in these lower regions near the earth: heaven is always clear and free from them. They are restrained by the ministry of angels, standing on the four corners of the earth, intimating that the spirit of error cannot go forth till God permits it, and that the angels minister to the good of the church by restraining its enemies. And their restraint was only for a season, and that was till the servants of God were sealed in their foreheads: God has a particular care and concern for his own servants in times of temptation and corruption, and he has a way to secure them from the common infection; he first establishes them, and then he tries them, for he has the timing of their trials in his own hand.

Give the chapter’s argument and then localise the vision. The four angels hold the four winds of heaven; the angel with the seal of the living God seals the servants of God out of the twelve tribes, whose number amounted to a hundred and forty-four thousand; besides these there was an innumerable multitude from all nations, who gave glory to God and the Lamb; and one of the elders shows who these are and describes their most happy state. After these things means immediately after the preceding vision. The four angels are instruments which God employs in the dispensation of his providence, though we know not what; the four corners of the earth are the extreme parts of the land of Judea, called the land or the earth by way of eminence; and holding the four winds means preventing evil from every quarter, keeping the whole of the land free from evil till the Church of Christ should wax strong, and each of his followers have time to prepare for his flight from Jerusalem, previously to its total destruction by the Romans. The angel with the seal is represented as the chancellor of the supreme King, ascending from the rising of the sun; some understand this of Christ, who is himself called the east. Or take the four angels the other way, as probably evil ones. They have their employ with the four first trumpets, as have other evil angels with the three last, and would willingly have brought on all the calamities that follow without delay; but they were restrained till the servants of God were sealed and the seven angels were ready to sound. They stand on the four corners of the earth — east, west, south, north — and in that order proceed the four first trumpets; and they hold the winds which else might have softened the fiery heat under the first, second and third trumpet. What follows is a preparation for the seventh seal, which is the weightiest of all. The plagues begin in the east, and so does the sealing.

Read the angels as kingdoms and the east as the Lord. The four angels are four principal kingdoms, namely of the Assyrians, and Persians, and Greeks, and Romans; and as in the former seals, after the manifold conflicts of the Church, he saw the joys of triumphant souls, so now also he is to prove by examples the victory over the preceding kingdoms of the world, which have now submitted to the Church of Christ. The winds in a manner stifled all things by their might, and suffered no one to breathe of his own free will; in the earth is signified the variety of provinces, in the sea of islands, in the trees the different quality and condition of men. Otherwise, by the four angels are to be understood four winds, according to the prophecy of Daniel, who says, Behold the four winds of heaven strove upon the great sea, and four beasts came up from the sea. The east is the Lord incarnate, who is the Angel of the great counsel, that is, the Messenger of his Father’s will, who has visited us, the day-spring from on high, bearing the ensign of the cross, with which to seal his own in their foreheads; and the loud voice is the cry lifted up on high, Repent ye, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Or take the angel to be a man. He speaks of Elias the prophet, who is the precursor of the times of Antichrist, for the restoration and establishment of the churches from the great and intolerable persecution; and we read that these things are predicted in the opening of the Old and New Testament, for God says by Malachi, Lo, I will send to you Elias the Tishbite, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. To that end he shows that the number of those that shall believe, of the Jews and of the nations, is a great multitude which no man was able to number.

debates: Whether the four angels are good or evil, and whether they are angels or kingdoms.
What the four winds are: persecution, error, or judgment.
What period the restraint covers.
Who the angel from the east is.
outliers: Wesley takes the four angels for evil ones, held back until the trumpets are ready to sound.
Bede reads them as the four kingdoms of Assyria, Persia, Greece and Rome.
Victorinus identifies the sealing angel with Elias, precursor of the times of Antichrist.
Gill dates the whole restraint to the peace of the church between Constantine and Theodosius.
Barnes declines to attach any meaning to the east, on the principle that not every detail of a symbol has a fulfilment.

3.pericope_label: Saying, Hurt not the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees, till we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads. And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel

schools.summary: Say what the command suspends and what the plural implies. Let the winds be restrained until what is designated shall be done: these destroying angels were commanded to suspend the work of destruction until the servants of God could be rendered secure, and the division of the earth, the sea and the trees seems to include everything — water, land, and the productions of the earth. Nothing was to be injured until the angel should designate the true servants of God. The use of the plural we seems to denote that he did not expect to do it alone; who were to be associated with him, whether angels or men, he does not intimate, but the work evidently demanded the agency of more than one. A mark placed on the forehead would be conspicuous, and would be something which could at once be recognised if destruction should spread over the world; the fulfilment is to be found in two things, in something conspicuous, so that it could be seen, and in a mark of such a character as would be a proper designation of the fact that they were the true servants of God. On the number, note first that he heard it: he does not say where he heard it, or by whom it was communicated, or when; the material point is that he heard it, and did not see it. Then ask whether the number is literal or symbolical, and answer that there is no good reason for doubt: the fair interpretation requires it to be symbolical, for the whole scene is symbolical — the winds, the angels, the sealing; it cannot be supposed that this number will include all who will be sealed and saved, since on whatever interpretation more than this will be saved; and the number is too exact and artificial to suppose it literal. Elsewhere put the questions the passage raises and answer them in order: what are we to understand by the number twelve thousand from each tribe, who are these who are drawn from the tribes of Israel, and why is there a change of the order and name of the tribes? Take the second first. Some have thought the sealed ones must be Jewish Christians, being disposed to take the twelve tribes literally; but the scope of the previous verses seems decisive against this view. The time of judgment and trial is drawing near, we have seen the tokens of the coming storm in the opening of the sixth seal, our wish is to know the lot of the saints of God, and this chapter answers that wish — they are safe, having the seal of God. To limit the answer to the Israelitish Christians is to break in abruptly upon the general flow of thought with a bold literalism: the sealed ones are explained to be the servants of God, and the description which follows proclaims them to be the Israel of God. Elsewhere again keep to the grammar. Hurt not is a prohibition with the ingressive aorist subjunctive, not to begin to hurt; till we shall have sealed is a temporal clause of indefinite future action, but there is no idea of completed action in the aorist subjunctive — simply, till we seal. Upon their foreheads comes from Ezekiel, the word being an old one meaning after or above the eye, the space above or between the eyes, and occurring in the New Testament only in this book. On the number: he did not see the sealing or count them himself, but only heard. It is symbolical, of course, and not meant to be a complete number of the sealed or saved even in that generation, let alone for all time; the number connotes perfection, twelve times twelve times a thousand. There are two opposite views, one taking the sealed as referring only to Jews, whether an actual remnant or Jewish Christians, the other including Gentiles as well, that is, the true Israel; this is the more probable view, and it takes the twelve tribes in a spiritual sense. But on either view a difficulty remains about the names of the tribes. The list is not geographical, since Levi is included, but Dan is omitted and Manasseh put in his place, though he, as the son of Joseph, is included in Joseph; and it was suggested in antiquity that Antichrist was expected to come from the tribe of Dan, and hence the omission.

Explain why the winds are only retarded. Their commission was not contradicted, nor taken away by Christ, for at the time appointed, at the blowing of the several trumpets, they let loose the winds, and let in the Goths, Huns and Vandals, the Saracens and Turks into the empire, and after that poured out the vials of God’s wrath upon the Romish antichrist. This retarding of them was but in appearance, that there might be an opportunity to show to John what care would be taken all along of the church of Christ, and of the true servants of the living God. On the number, note how it was known: he heard the number of them which were sealed, and therefore could be sure of the exact number, which did not depend upon his sight, and his telling them, in which some mistake might have been made, but he heard the number expressed.

Take the sealing as consecration and protection. There is manifestly an allusion here to Ezekiel: by sealing we are to understand consecrating the persons in a more especial manner to God, and showing, by this mark of God upon them, that they were under his more immediate protection, and that nothing should hurt them. It was a custom in the east, and indeed in the west too, to stamp with a hot iron the name of the owner upon the forehead or shoulder of his slave. And it is worthy of remark that not one Christian perished in the siege of Jerusalem: all had left the city and escaped to Pella. On the number, say that in the hundred and forty-four thousand are included all the Jews converted to Christianity, twelve thousand out of each of the twelve tribes; but this must be only a certain number put for an uncertain one, for it is not to be supposed that just twelve thousand were converted out of each tribe. Elsewhere note that other angels were joined in commission with the first, and that to have sealed the servants of God on their foreheads means to have secured the servants of God of the twelve tribes from the impending calamities, whereby they shall be as clearly distinguished from the rest as if they were visibly marked on their foreheads. Of the children of Israel: to these will afterwards be joined a multitude out of all nations. But observe that this is not the number of all the Israelites who are saved from Abraham or Moses to the end of all things, but only of those who were secured from the plagues which were then ready to fall on the earth; and it seems as if this book had, in many places, a special view to the people of Israel.

debates: Who the we of the sealing angel includes.
Whether the hundred and forty-four thousand is a literal number.
Whether the sealed are Jewish Christians or the whole church.
Why Dan is omitted from the list of tribes and Manasseh put in his place.
outliers: Clarke cites the escape of the Christians to Pella as the fulfilment of the sealing.
Gill reads the restraint as a delay before the trumpets loose the barbarian invasions.
Wesley confines the sealed to Israelites secured from the plagues then impending.
Robertson reports the ancient explanation that Dan was omitted because Antichrist was expected from that tribe.

5.pericope_label: Of the tribe of Juda were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Reuben were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Gad were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Aser were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Nepthalim were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Manasses were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Simeon were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Levi were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Issachar were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Zabulon were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Joseph were sealed twelve thousand. Of the tribe of Benjamin were sealed twelve thousand

schools.summary: Read the roll as a figure of the whole church. A selection was made, or a number sealed, as if it had been made from one of the tribes of the children of Israel; and this refers to the Christian church, meaning that each portion of the church would furnish a definite part of the whole number sealed and saved. We are not required to understand this of the exact number of twelve thousand, but that the designation would be made from all parts and branches of the church, as if a selection of the true servants of God were made from the whole number of the tribes of Israel. There seems to be no particular reason why the tribe of Judah was mentioned first: Judah was not the oldest of the sons of Jacob, and there was no settled order in which the tribes were usually mentioned. The order of their birth in Genesis is Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin; in the blessing of Jacob this order is changed to Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Joseph, Benjamin; and in the blessing of Moses a different order still is observed. Then look for the fact answering to the figure, and find it first in the preservation of the church from extinction during those calamitous periods when ruin seemed about to sweep over the Roman world. Not only was there a suspension of those impending judgments that seemed to threaten the very extinction of the empire by the invasion of the Northern hordes, but there were special acts in favour of the church, by which these fierce barbarians appeared not only to be restrained from destroying the church, but to be influenced by tenderness and sympathy for it, as if they were raised up to preserve it when Rome had done all it could to destroy it. It would seem as if God restrained the rage of these hordes for the sake of preserving his church, and as if he had touched their hearts that they might give to Christians an opportunity to escape in the impending storm. Refer particularly to the conduct of Alaric, king of the Goths, in the sack of Rome; and take the account from a historian who will not be suspected of a design to contribute anything to the illustration of the Apocalypse.

Construe the names, and make each a lesson for the sealed. Judah is mentioned first because Christ sprang from that tribe, and the pure worship of God was preserved in it, and it was preserved a distinct tribe until the coming of Shiloh; its name signifies praise God, and shows that it becomes all the sealed ones, all true believers, and every member of the church of God, to praise him for all favours and blessings, temporal, spiritual and eternal. Asher, which the Septuagint pronounce Aser, signifies blessed, as all the sealed ones are, blessed with all spiritual blessings, with grace here and glory hereafter. Simeon signifies hearing, and such a hearing as is attended with obedience, denoting the spiritual and practical hearing of the Gospel by those who hear, and understand, and believe, and practise what they hear, and yield the obedience of faith unto it. Zebulun signifies dwelling, and was the tribe in which Christ had his dwelling, and where he much conversed; and it may denote his gracious inhabitation, as well as that of God the Father and of the Spirit, among the saints and sealed ones.

Note three things about the list, and then account for the omissions. First, the tribe of Levi is here mentioned, though that tribe had no inheritance in Israel; but they now belonged to the spiritual priesthood. Secondly, the tribe of Dan, which had an inheritance, is here omitted, as also the tribe of Ephraim. Thirdly, the tribe of Joseph is here added in the place of Ephraim; and Ephraim and Dan, being the principal promoters of idolatry, are left out in this enumeration. Say also why Judah stands first: in respect of the kingdom, and of the Messiah sprung therefrom. On Levi, add that after the Levitical ceremonies were abolished, Levi was again on a level with his brethren. On Joseph, that he is named perhaps for Ephraim, as having been, with Dan, the most idolatrous of all the tribes. And on Dan, add what is further observable: that it was very early reduced to a single family, which family itself seems to have been cut off in war before the time of Ezra; for in the Chronicles, where the posterity of the patriarchs is recited, Dan is wholly omitted.

debates: Why Judah is named first.
Why Dan and Ephraim are omitted and Joseph put in.
Whether the twelve thousands are exact numbers.
What historical fact answers to the sealing.
outliers: Gill construes each tribal name as a spiritual lesson for the sealed.
Barnes denies that any reason can be given for the order, and sets three biblical lists against each other.
Wesley reports that the tribe of Dan had died out before the time of Ezra.
Barnes finds the fulfilment in the barbarian invaders sparing the church, and cites Gibbon for it.

9.pericope_label: After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands; and cried with a loud voice, saying, Salvation to our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb. And all the angels stood round about the throne, and about the elders and the four beasts, and fell before the throne on their faces, and worshipped God, saying, Amen: Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honour, and power, and might, be unto our God for ever and ever. Amen

schools.summary: Distinguish this vision from the last. After these things means that after he had seen those things thus represented, he had another vision, which implies not only that he saw it afterwards but that it would occur subsequently; though whether immediately, or with other things intervening, is not stated. The vision seems transferred from earth to heaven, for the multitudes appeared before the throne of God; and the design is to carry the mind forward quite beyond the storms and tempests of earth, the scenes of woe and sorrow, the days of error, darkness, declension and persecution, into that period when the church should be triumphant in heaven. Instead, therefore, of leaving the impression that the hundred and forty-four thousand would be all that would be saved, the eye is directed to an innumerable host, gathered from all ages, all climes and all people, triumphant in glory: the multitude seen was not the same as the hundred and forty-four thousand, but a far greater number, the whole assembled host of the redeemed. On the cry, guard the words: it cannot mean, as the English would seem to imply, that they desired that God might have salvation, but that their salvation was to be attributed solely to him. The word means properly safety, deliverance, preservation, then welfare or prosperity, then victory, then in a Christian sense deliverance from punishment and admission to eternal life; and one lexicographer renders it here victory. Whatever is included in the word will be due to God alone — deliverance from sin, danger and death, the triumph over every foe, the resurrection from the grave, the rescue from eternal burnings, and the admission to glory. On the angels, note that they stood in the outer circle, outside the elders and the four living creatures, the redeemed occupying the inner circle near the throne; they sympathise with the church redeemed and triumphant as they did with the church in its conflicts and trials, and see in that redemption new displays of the character of God. Amen is a word strongly affirming the truth of what is said, or expressing hearty assent to it. Elsewhere set the two visions against each other as stages. We have just had the picture of the sealing of a multitude which could be numbered; now we have the picture of a countless throng. Are they the same, or others? The answer is that this vision gives the climax of the previous one: the sealing represented the Passover of the Church, this vision represents its Feast of Tabernacles. The sealing assured us that in the midst of the severe times of testing there would be those who, wearing God’s armour, would come forth unscathed; this vision shows us the fruition of their labour and their rest after conflict. The sealing assured us that God’s hidden ones would be safe in trouble; this tells us that they have come safe out of it, being those who have come out of the great tribulation. On the cry, take the salvation in its most comprehensive sense, including every deliverance — from the curse of law, from the power of sin, and from the perils of life — and note the recurrence of the Lamb: they are before the throne and before the Lamb, and their salvation is ascribed to God and to the Lamb. On the doxology, the sevenfold form implies a divine completeness, appropriate to this vision, which shows the close of the Church’s agony; and it is in itself a slight indication that the view which would limit the seals to some short period of Church history is incorrect, as it is assuredly inadequate. Elsewhere again keep to the grammar. The list of nations, kindreds, peoples and tongues gives a polyglott cosmopolitan crowd. Standing is nominative masculine plural referring to a masculine singular noun, a construction according to sense; arrayed is accusative rather than nominative, a common variation in this book, which one editor regards as a mere slip that would have been corrected had the writer read his manuscript over. They cry is a vivid dramatic present, and the polyglott multitude shouts its praises as with one voice. Salvation is a nominative absolute, regarded as an accomplished act on the part of those coming out of the great tribulation, and the praise for it is given both to God and to the Lamb, who are thus both called Saviour, as in the Pastoral Epistles. Were standing is a past perfect used like an imperfect; the angels here rejoice in the salvation of men; and note the Amen at the beginning and at the close of the doxology, with a separate article before each of the seven attributes given to God.

Say what this vision is not, and then when it is. What follows is a distinct vision from the preceding one, and not a continuation of it, as if the sealing of the Jewish believers were designed by the former and the sealing of the Gentiles by this; for in this vision there is no mention made of sealing, nor was there, or will there be, any need of it in the time it refers to. Nor is it the time of the Reformation, nor when the vials began to be poured out upon the seat of the beast; for though there were great numbers converted in many nations, kindreds, people and tongues, yet not in all; and the characters of this great multitude, and the happiness they shall enjoy, do not seem to suit with persons in a state of mortality and imperfection. Wherefore many interpreters understand this vision of the saints in heaven; but it rather respects the millennium state, or thousand years’ reign of Christ with his saints on earth, with which all that is here said agrees. On the cry, note that they cried with a loud voice to show the strength of their affection and the greatness of their joy, and how sensible they were of the favour they enjoyed, and how hearty in the ascription of glory to God and the Lamb. On the angels, note that these are the holy and elect angels, even all of them, the ten thousand times ten thousand and thousands of thousands, the innumerable company of them; and that in saying Amen they approve and confirm what the great multitude had said in ascribing the glory of salvation to God and the Lamb — for though they have no part in it themselves, they yet highly approve it as right and just that men should give the glory of it where it is due.

Set the two companies in order and then draw the use. The first fruits of Christ having led the way, the Gentiles converted later follow, and ascribe their salvation to God and the Redeemer with triumph. In acts of religious worship we come nigh to God, and must come by Christ: the throne of God could not be approached by sinners were it not for a Mediator. They were clothed with the robes of justification, holiness and victory, and they had palms in their hands, as conquerors used to appear in their triumphs; and such a glorious appearance will the faithful servants of God make at last, when they have fought the good fight of faith and finished their course. With a loud voice they gave to God and the Lamb the praise of the great salvation. Those who enjoy eternal happiness must and will bless both the Father and the Son; they will do it publicly, and with fervour. We see what is the work of heaven, and we ought to begin it now, to have our hearts much in it, and to long for that world where our praises, as well as our happiness, will be made perfect.

Identify the multitude and read the tokens. This appears to mean the Church of Christ among the Gentiles, for it was different from that collected from the twelve tribes, and it is here said to be of all nations, kindreds, people and tongues. They are clothed with white robes as emblems of innocence and purity, and have palms in their hands in token of victory gained over the world, the devil and the flesh. Salvation to our God means that God alone is the author of the salvation of man, and this salvation is procured for and given to them through the Lamb, as their propitiatory sacrifice. As there is joy in the presence of God among the holy angels when one sinner repents, no wonder that they take such an interest in the gathering together of such innumerable multitudes who are fully saved from their sins; and in the doxology there are seven different species of praise attributed to God. Elsewhere say who the multitude are and digress on their reward. They are those who had happily finished their course; such multitudes are described afterwards, and still higher degrees of glory which they attain after a sharp fight and magnificent victory. There is an inconceivable variety in the degrees of reward in the other world. Let not any slothful one say, if I get to heaven at all, I will be content: such an one may let heaven go altogether. In worldly things men are ambitious to get as high as they can; Christians have a far more noble ambition. The difference between the very highest and the lowest state in the world is nothing to the smallest difference between the degrees of glory. But who has time to think of this? Who is at all concerned about it? Standing before the throne means in the full vision of God, and the palms are tokens of joy and victory. On the angels: they stood in waiting, the living creatures next the throne, the elders round these, and the angels round them both; and they fell on their faces, as the elders do once only later — the heavenly ceremonial has its fixed order and measure. With the Amen all the angels confirm the words of the great multitude, but they likewise carry the praise much higher: before the Lamb began to open the seven seals a sevenfold hymn of praise was brought him by many angels, and now, as he is upon opening the last seal, all the angels give sevenfold praise to God.

debates: Whether the great multitude is the same company as the sealed hundred and forty-four thousand.
Whether the scene is in heaven, in the millennium, or on earth.
What salvation to our God means.
What the sevenfold doxology implies about the scope of the seals.
outliers: Gill refers the vision to the millennial reign on earth rather than to heaven.
Ellicott reads the two visions as the Passover and the Feast of Tabernacles of the Church.
Wesley digresses on the degrees of reward and rebukes those content merely to reach heaven.
Barnes reports that one lexicographer renders the word salvation here simply as victory.

13.pericope_label: And one of the elders answered, saying unto me, What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they? And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb

schools.summary: Explain the idiom first. Answer, with us, means to reply to something which has been said; in the Bible the word is not unfrequently used at the beginning of a speech where nothing has been said, as if it were a reply to something that might be said, or to something passing through the mind of another. John was looking on the host and reflecting on the state of things, and to the train of thought passing through his mind the elder answered by an inquiry. The object is to bring the case of these persons more particularly into view: the vast host with branches of palm had attracted the attention of John, but the speaker turns his thoughts to a particular part of the host, the martyrs who stood among them, with an emphasis on these. There was a propriety in thus directing the mind to the martyrs as triumphing in heaven, in a time when the churches were suffering persecution, and in view of the vision of darkness and calamity at the opening of the sixth seal. Sir is a form of respectful address such as would be used when speaking to a superior, and thou knowest is a modest confession that he did not know, with the opinion that his questioner did. Tribulation is a word of general character, meaning affliction, though perhaps there is here an allusion to persecution; the sense would be better expressed by great trials, and the object was to set before the mind those who had suffered much and by their sufferings had been sanctified, in order to encourage those who might yet be called to suffer. There is some incongruity in saying that they made their robes white in blood, and the meaning therefore must be that they cleansed them in it: under the ancient ritual various things about the sanctuary were cleansed from ceremonial defilement by the sprinkling of the blood of sacrifice. It is not said that they were made white as the result of their sufferings, but by the blood of the Lamb, and this is one of the incidental proofs of the reality of the atonement. If he shed his blood merely as other men have done, if he died only as a martyr, what propriety would there have been in referring to his blood more than to the blood of any other martyr, and what influence could that blood have in cleansing the robes of the saints in heaven? Such language would be unmeaning; it is never used except in connexion with the blood of Christ. Elsewhere answer the unspoken question. The seer had asked no question, but the elder answers the wondering thoughts and questionings which fill his mind, and asks the question which he knows the apostle would fain ask; perhaps this scene was in Dante’s mind when he described himself in Paradise as silent, yet with desire painted in his looks. The question brings the white robes into prominence: he recognises the multitudes as men and women out of every nation and tribe of sinful humanity, and sees them clothed in the garb of holiness. The form of the reply shows how completely the elder had anticipated his thoughts, for it is described as instantaneous; my Lord is the language of reverent regard, but not of worship. Read the present tense: these are those coming out of the great tribulation, not all at once but gradually, for the saints of God are continually passing into the unseen world. There is no doubt about the emphasis the definite article gives, but while there may yet be trials so great that they may be called the great tribulation, it seems out of harmony with the spirit of the book to limit the phrase to some special season. Is it not rather the tribulation which those must encounter who are on the side of Christ and righteousness and refuse to receive the mark of worldliness and sin on their heart, conscience and life? The vision is of the great multitude from every age and every race who waged war against sin. Read washed, not have washed, for the washing was done during their earthly life; the imagery is found in the Gospel and in the Epistle, and its use here points to a common authorship, being a following out of the words quoted from John the Baptist, the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world. Elsewhere keep to the grammar. Answered is a first aorist passive deponent with a participle of saying, a common Hebrew redundancy in the Gospels but found only here in the Apocalypse; an elder intervenes, though no question has been asked, to interpret the vision. These is a prophetic predicate nominative put before who are they, and the article is repeated pointing back to the robes of the earlier verse. I say is a perfect active indicative: to the seer’s mind the whole scene was still fresh and vivid, not the so-called aoristic perfect. My lord is an address of reverence to a heavenly being, not an act of worship; thou knowest is at once a confession of ignorance and an appeal for information. They which come is a present middle participle with the idea of continued repetition, so that the martyrs are still arriving from the scene of the great tribulation; apparently some great crisis is contemplated, though the whole series may be in mind. The change of construction to and they washed is common in this book, one of its Hebraisms. Made them white is a first aorist active of a verb found in the New Testament only here and in one Gospel; the language comes partly from Genesis and partly from Exodus, and the aorists look back to the life on earth when the cleansing was effected. There is power alone in the blood of Christ to cleanse from sin, not in the blood of the martyrs themselves, and the result is white, not red, as one might imagine.

Ask who the elder is, and refuse to settle it. This elder was not the Apostle Peter, as some interpreters have thought, and still less Pope Silvester, who lived in the times of Constantine; he is much more likely, according to others, to be Constantine himself, the first of the elders, or the chief magistrate when the church sprung out of its troubles and enjoyed rest and peace; though some have thought of the prophet Isaiah, since many things said by this elder are to be found in his prophecy. But it is needless to inquire who the particular person was; it is enough to say that he was one of the four and twenty elders about the throne, one that belonged to the church, who in a visionary way is represented as accosting John upon the above sight. The word answered is a common Hebraism of the New Testament, which is often used when nothing goes before to which a return is made, and only signifies here that the elder opened his mouth, began to speak, and called to John. John replies in a very humble, modest and respectful manner, calling him Sir, according to the usage of the eastern people; and it is observable that this word is much used in his Gospel, more than in any other book. Some copies read my Lord, and so do the Latin, Syriac and Arabic versions. John confesses his ignorance and ascribes knowledge to the elder, and desires information of him; for the sense is that the elder knew who they were and from whence they came, but he did not, and therefore desires that he would inform him — one version renders it, my Lord, thou art more learned, that is, than I am, and therefore instruct me, as he accordingly did.

Take the question, the reply and the account in order, and draw a use from each. The question is asked by one of the elders, not for his own information but for John’s instruction: ministers may learn from the people, especially from aged and experienced Christians, for the lowest saint in heaven knows more than the greatest apostle in the world. It seems to be spoken by way of admiration, as when it is asked who is this that cometh out of the wilderness; faithful Christians deserve our notice and respect, and we should mark the upright. In the answer returned the apostle tacitly acknowledges his own ignorance and sues to this elder for information: those who would gain knowledge must not be ashamed to own their ignorance, nor to desire instruction from any that are able to give it. Then comes the account of that noble army of martyrs who stood before the throne in white robes with palms of victory in their hands. Note first the low and desolate state they had formerly been in: they had been in great tribulation, persecuted by men, tempted by Satan, sometimes troubled in their own spirits; they had suffered the spoiling of their goods, the imprisonment of their persons, yea the loss of life itself. The way to heaven lies through many tribulations, but tribulation, how great soever, shall not separate us from the love of God, and when gone through well it will make heaven more welcome and more glorious. Note next the means by which they were prepared for the honour they now enjoy: they had washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. It is not the blood of the martyrs themselves, but the blood of the Lamb, that can wash away sin and make the soul pure and clean in the sight of God; other blood stains, this is the only blood that makes the robes of the saints white and clean.

Give the plain sense and guard it. One of the elders answered is a Hebraism for spoke; the question is here asked that the proposer may have the opportunity of answering it. Sir, thou knowest means, I do not know, but thou canst inform me. Came out of great tribulation means persecutions of every kind, and have washed their robes means that they have obtained their pardon and purity through the blood of the Lamb. But their white robes cannot mean the righteousness of Christ, for this cannot be washed and made white in his own blood. This white linen is said elsewhere in the book to be the righteousness of the saints, and this is the righteousness in which they stand before the throne; therefore it is not Christ’s righteousness, but a righteousness wrought in them by the merit of his blood and the power of his Spirit. Elsewhere set the passage in its place and widen the multitude. What stands in these verses to the end of the chapter might have immediately followed the tenth verse, but that the praise of the angels, which was at the same time with that of the great multitude, came in between; and answered means that he answered John’s desire to know, not any words that he spoke. My lord, or my master, is a common term of respect, as Zechariah likewise bespeaks the angel; thou knowest means, I know not, but thou dost. These are they — not martyrs, for these are not such a multitude as no man can number; but as all the angels appear here, so do all the souls of the righteous who had lived from the beginning of the world. He does not say who did come, but who come now also, to whom likewise pertain all who will come hereafter. Out of great affliction, of various kinds, wisely and graciously allotted by God to all his children; and have washed their robes from all guilt, and made them white in all holiness, by the blood of the Lamb, which not only cleanses but adorns us also.

debates: Who the elder is, and whether the question is asked for his own sake or for John’s.
Whether the multitude is the martyrs only or all the righteous of every age.
Whether the great tribulation is a final crisis or the lifelong conflict of the faithful.
Whether the white robes are the imputed righteousness of Christ or a righteousness wrought in the saints.
outliers: Gill canvasses Constantine and Isaiah as candidates for the elder before refusing to decide.
Wesley denies outright that these are martyrs, since martyrs could be numbered.
Clarke argues the robes cannot be Christ’s righteousness, since that could not be washed in his own blood.
Ellicott quotes Dante’s Paradiso for the desire that speaks without words.
Barnes makes the washing an incidental proof of the atonement.

15.pericope_label: Therefore are they before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple: and he that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them. They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat. For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters: and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes

schools.summary: Ground the reason and then unfold the images. The reason why they are there is to be traced to the fact that the Lamb shed his blood to make expiation for sin; no other reason can be given why any one of the human race is in heaven, and that is reason enough why any of that race are there. They serve him day and night, that is, continually: day and night constitute the whole of time, and this denotes constant and uninterrupted service. On earth toil is suspended by the return of night, and the service of God is intermitted by the necessity of rest; in heaven, as there will be no weariness, there will be no need of intermission, and the service of God, varied doubtless to meet the state of the mind, will be continued for ever. To serve him in his temple refers to heaven regarded as the holy dwelling-place of God. The word rendered dwell among them properly means to tent, to pitch a tent, and the allusion is perhaps to the tabernacle in the wilderness, which was regarded as the peculiar dwelling-place of God. A considerable portion of the redeemed were, when on the earth, subjected to the evils of famine, and many perished with hunger; in heaven they will be subjected to that evil no more, for the spiritual bodies they will have will doubtless be nourished in some other way than by food, if they require nourishment at all. As multitudes have been subjected to hunger, so have multitudes been subjected to the pains of thirst — in prison, in pathless deserts, in times of drought when wells and fountains were dried up — a cause producing as intense suffering perhaps as any that man endures. The words are taken from the prophet, who said that they shall not hunger nor thirst, neither shall the heat nor sun smite them. Shall feed them is rather, shall exercise over them the office of a shepherd, which includes much more than mere feeding: it embraces all the care which a shepherd takes of his flock, watching them, providing for them, guarding them from danger. Living fountains refer to running streams, as contrasted with standing water and stagnant pools; no image of happiness is more vivid, or would be more striking to an Oriental, than that of such fountains flowing in sandy and burning wastes. The word living must refer to the fact that that happiness will be perennial: these fountains will always bubble, these streams will never dry up. The wiping away of tears is a new image taken from another place in the same prophet, and is one of exquisite tenderness. Of all the negative descriptions of heaven there is no one perhaps better adapted to produce consolation than this. This is a world of weeping, a vale of tears. Philosophers have sought a brief definition of man and have sought in vain; would there be any better description of him, as representing the reality of his condition here, than to say that he is one who weeps? Who of the human family has not shed a tear over the grave of a friend, over his own losses and cares, over his sins? What a change would it make in our world if hence forward not another tear would be shed. Elsewhere read the passage by the tabernacle. On this account are they before the throne, that is, because they so washed their robes; and the life is not simply one of joy or safety, it is one also of service. Those who were made priests to God here carry on their service in his temple; yet this can only be figurative language, for in the heavenly city there is no temple. It serves to teach us that the servant will find his fitting work of service there as well as here. Shall dwell among them does not do justice to the word, and at the same time obscures the allusion which the seer has in mind. The allusion is to the Shechinah, the symbol of the Divine Presence which rested over the mercy seat; the idea that it would be restored once more in Messiah’s days was a cherished hope of the Jewish doctors during and after the apostolic ages. He will tabernacle over them; there seems also to be a carrying on of the imagery derived from the Feast of Tabernacles, for as there were the palm branches of the harvest joy, so there will be the booth of God’s presence among them. He shall be their pavilion, their shelter, a tabernacle for a shadow in the day-time from the heat, and for a covert from storm and from rain. The negatives of the next verse are emphatic and rise in force as the verse proceeds: none of the privations endured for Christ’s sake shall trouble them, and then too shall that blessed hunger and thirst for righteousness be appeased. The Eastern sun, in its fierce and overpowering intensity, was a fit emblem of those trials which dry up the springs of strength. The Lamb is described as in the midst of the throne, the central object immediately in front of it, so that he who would draw near to the throne must pass the Lamb; the word translated feed means to tend as a shepherd tends his flock, and the twenty-third Psalm rises at once to our minds. Significantly the springs of this living water are in the throne itself; one prophet saw the stream issuing forth from the temple, but in the city where there is no temple we are carried to the very throne of God. In the emblem of the water we have another allusion to the Feast of Tabernacles, when the priest drew a vessel of water from the brook of Siloam and poured it out by the altar of burnt offering while the people sang that with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation. In the prophet it is said God shall wipe away tears from off all faces; here it is every tear, so that no tears shall gather in any eye, for the sources of sorrow will be cut off in the land where there is no more sin. Only those who have wept can enjoy this consolation; who would not shed life’s tears to have God’s hand to wipe them away? Elsewhere keep to the words. Therefore means because of the washing just described. They serve him takes a dative with a verb that meant originally to serve for hire, then service in general, then religious service to God, then in particular the ritual worship of the priests. All the redeemed are priests in the heavenly temple, but this service is that of spiritual worship, not of external rites. Day and night is a genitive of time. Shall spread his tabernacle over them is a future active of a verb from the noun for tent, used in the Gospel of the earthly life of Christ and elsewhere in the New Testament only in this book: here of God spreading his tent over the redeemed in heaven, later of God tabernacling with them, in both instances a picture of sacred fellowship, with the further idea of God’s presence as a protection from all fear of evil, like the overshadowing of Israel by the Shekinah. They shall hunger no more is a free translation of the prophet, not a quotation from the Greek version; the two strong human appetites will be gone, a clear refutation of a gross materialistic or sensual conception of the future life. Neither shall strike uses a strong double negative: they will no longer be under the rays of the sun as upon earth. Heat is an old word from the verb to burn, painful and burning heat. In the midst answers to the position of the Lamb given earlier. Shall be their shepherd is a future active of the verb from the noun for shepherd; Jesus is still the Good Shepherd of his sheep. Shall guide them uses a verb used of God’s guidance of Israel, of God’s guidance of individual lives, and of the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Note the order, to life’s water springs, with the emphasis on life’s.

Fix the ground and then the place of the Lamb. They are before the throne of God, not because of their great tribulations, but because they were brought through them, and out of them, by the grace and power of God; nor because of their robes, or conversation garments, but because those were washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb, or because of the blood of the Lamb and their justification, pardon and cleansing by it. They shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more: the words are taken from the prophet, and will be true in a literal and corporeal sense, for now the saints are often in hunger and thirst, and then they shall be so no more. In a mystical and spiritual sense there will be no famine of the word; for though there will not be the outward ministration of the word as now, the substance of it will be enjoyed to full satisfaction, nor will there be any uneasy desires after spiritual things, and much less any hungerings and thirstings, or lusting after carnal, sensual and earthly things. For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne: not before the throne, as the great multitude are said to be; nor round about it, as the angels are; but in the midst of it, being equal to him that sits upon it, sitting on the same throne with him, and having the same power and authority.

Give the plain sense, and then let the images open. Therefore, because they are washed in the blood of the Lamb, are they before the throne, admitted to the immediate presence of God; and serve him day and night, without ceasing, being filled with the spirit of prayer, faith, love and obedience. Shall dwell among them: he lives in his own Church, and in the heart of every true believer. They shall hunger no more, that is, they shall no longer be deprived of their religious ordinances and the blessings attendant on them, as they were when in a state of persecution. Neither shall the sun light on them: their secular rulers, being converted to God, became nursing fathers to the Church; nor any heat, neither persecution nor affliction of any kind, which the Hebrews express by the terms heat and scorching. Shall feed them means that he shall communicate to them every thing calculated to secure, continue and increase their happiness. A spring in the Hebrew phraseology is termed living water, because constantly boiling up and running on, and by these perpetual fountains we are to understand endless sources of comfort and happiness which Jesus Christ will open out of his own infinite plenitude to all glorified souls. These eternal living fountains will make an infinite variety in the enjoyments of the blessed: there will be no sameness, and consequently no cloying with the perpetual enjoyment of the same things; every moment will open a new source of pleasure, instruction and improvement, and they shall make an eternal progression into the fullness of God. As God is infinite, so his attributes are infinite, and throughout infinity more and more of those attributes will be discovered, and the discovery of each will be a new fountain of enjoyment; these sources must be opening through all eternity, and yet through all eternity there will still remain an infinity of them to be opened. This is one of the finest images in the Bible. God shall wipe away, in the most affectionate and fatherly manner, all tears from their eyes, all causes of distress and grief: they shall have pure, unmixed happiness. Elsewhere keep it short and warm. Therefore, because they came out of great affliction and have washed their robes in his blood, are they before the throne — it seems, even nearer than the angels — and serve him day and night, speaking after the manner of men, that is, continually, in his temple, which is in heaven; and he shall have his tent over them, shall spread his glory over them as a covering. Neither shall the sun light on them, for God is there their sun; nor any painful heat, or inclemency of seasons. The Lamb will feed them with eternal peace and joy, so that they shall hunger no more, and will lead them to living fountains of water, the comforts of the Holy Ghost, so that they shall thirst no more; neither shall they suffer or grieve any more, for God will wipe away all tears from their eyes.

debates: Whether their place before the throne rests on their sufferings or only on the blood of the Lamb.
Whether the heavenly service is priestly and ritual or spiritual worship only.
Whether the promised freedom from sun and heat is a heavenly condition or the historical relief of the Church under converted rulers.
Whether the hunger and thirst removed are bodily, spiritual, or both.
outliers: Clarke reads the sun that shall not light on them as secular rulers turned nursing fathers to the Church.
Ellicott traces the tabernacling to the Shechinah and to the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles.
Gill argues the Lamb is in the midst of the throne rather than before it because he is equal to him that sits on it.
Clarke turns the living fountains into an eternal progression into the fullness of God.
Barnes proposes that man might be defined as the creature that weeps.
